title: Polarity of water
body: Water is polar because polar covalent bonds form between hydrogen and oxygen within each water molecule, which contributes to hydrogen bonding between and within biological molecules.
caution: Polar covalent bonds are within a water molecule; hydrogen bonds are between molecules (or within large biological molecules). Do not call hydrogen bonds covalent.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.1.i "Water has polarity, because of the formation of polar covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen within water molecules"

title: Hydrogen bonding
body: Hydrogen bonding is the attraction between polar molecules (or polar regions of molecules) that results from polarity, and it occurs between and within biological molecules.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.1.i "contributes to hydrogen bonding between and within biological molecules"; 1.6.A.3; 1.7.A.4; 1.7.A.5

title: High specific heat capacity of water
body: Water has a high specific heat capacity, which allows for the maintenance of homeostatic body temperature within living organisms.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.1.ii "Water has a high specific heat capacity"

title: High heat of vaporization of water
body: Water has a high heat of vaporization, which allows evaporative cooling of the surrounding environment and helps maintain body temperature in living organisms.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.1.iii "Water has a high heat of vaporization"

title: Properties from hydrogen bonds between adjacent water molecules
body: Hydrogen bonds between adjacent polar water molecules result in these three properties.

items.label: Cohesion
items.meaning: Result of hydrogen bonds between adjacent water molecules

items.label: Adhesion
items.meaning: Result of hydrogen bonds between adjacent polar water molecules

items.label: Surface tension
items.meaning: Result of hydrogen bonds between adjacent polar water molecules

ced_evidence: 1.1.A.2 "result in cohesion, adhesion, and surface tension"

title: Elements used to build biological molecules
body: C, H, and O are most prevalent in carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids; S, P, and N have specific uses.

items.label: Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen
items.meaning: Most prevalent elements in carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids

items.label: Sulfur
items.meaning: Used in the building of proteins

items.label: Phosphorus
items.meaning: Used in the building of phospholipids (a type of lipid) and nucleic acids

items.label: Nitrogen
items.meaning: Used in the building of nucleic acids

ced_evidence: 1.2.A.1 "Carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen are the most prevalent elements"

title: Dehydration synthesis
body: Dehydration synthesis joins two smaller molecules by covalent bonding when a hydrogen ion is removed from one monomer and a hydroxyl group from the other, losing the equivalent of a water molecule; connecting many monomers is polymerization.
caution: State that a hydrogen ion and a hydroxyl group are removed (the equivalent of water is lost) and a covalent bond forms between the two monomers.
ced_evidence: 1.3.A.2 "loss of the equivalent of a water molecule from the reactants"

title: Hydrolysis
body: Hydrolysis is a chemical reaction that cleaves covalent bonds, breaking molecules into smaller molecules; when water is added to the bond between monomers in a polymer, the hydrogen ion goes to one monomer and the hydroxyl group to the other.
caution: Say that water is added to the bond, with H going to one monomer and OH to the other; do not say water is released.
ced_evidence: 1.3.A.1 "When water is added to the bond between monomers in a polymer, the bond is broken"

title: Monosaccharides and polysaccharides
body: Monosaccharides (simple sugars) are the monomers for polysaccharides (complex carbohydrates), which are polymers joined by covalent bonds and may be linear or branched.
ced_evidence: 1.4.A.1 "Monosaccharides (simple sugars) are the monomers for polysaccharides (complex carbohydrates)"

title: Illustrative polysaccharides
body: Examples of complex carbohydrates named for EK 1.4.A.1.

items.label: Cellulose
items.meaning: Polysaccharide (polymer of monosaccharides)

items.label: Starch
items.meaning: Polysaccharide (polymer of monosaccharides)

items.label: Glycogen
items.meaning: Polysaccharide (polymer of monosaccharides)

ced_evidence: EK 1.4.A.1 illustrative examples: Cellulose, Starch, Glycogen

title: Lipids
body: Lipids are typically nonpolar, hydrophobic molecules whose structure and function derive from how their subcomponents are assembled.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.1 "Lipids are typically nonpolar, hydrophobic molecules"

title: Saturated vs. unsaturated fatty acids
body: Saturated fatty acids contain only single bonds between carbon atoms, whereas unsaturated fatty acids contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond, which causes the carbon chain to kink.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.1.i-ii "Saturated fatty acids contain only single bonds between carbon atoms"

title: Unsaturation and physical state
body: The more double bonds in a fatty acid tail, the more unsaturated the lipid, and the more unsaturated a lipid is, the more liquid it is at room temperature.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.1.iii-iv "The more unsaturated a lipid is, the more liquid it is at room temperature"

title: Lipid examples and their functions
body: Lipid types named in the CED with their functions.

items.label: Fats
items.meaning: Provide energy storage and support cell function; can provide insulation to keep mammals warm

items.label: Steroids
items.meaning: Hormones that support growth and development, energy metabolism, and homeostasis

items.label: Cholesterol
items.meaning: Provides essential structural stability to animal cell membranes

items.label: Phospholipids
items.meaning: Group together to form the lipid bilayers of plasma and cell membranes

ced_evidence: 1.5.A.2 "fats, steroids including cholesterol, and phospholipids"

title: Components of a nucleotide
body: Each nucleotide monomer of a nucleic acid has three structural components; information is encoded in the sequence of nucleotides.

items.label: Five-carbon sugar
items.meaning: Deoxyribose (DNA) or ribose (RNA)

items.label: Phosphate
items.meaning: Phosphate group of the nucleotide

items.label: Nitrogenous base
items.meaning: Adenine, thymine, guanine, cytosine, or uracil

ced_evidence: 1.6.A.1 "a five-carbon sugar (deoxyribose or ribose), a phosphate, and a nitrogenous base"

title: Nucleic acid strand direction: 5' and 3' ends
body: A nucleic acid strand's ends are defined by the 3' hydroxyl and 5' phosphate of the sugar, and during synthesis nucleotides are added to the 3' end of the growing strand, forming covalent bonds between nucleotides.
ced_evidence: 1.6.A.2 "nucleotides are added to the 3' end of the growing strand"

title: Complementary base pairing
body: In DNA, A pairs with T and C pairs with G via hydrogen bonds; in RNA, A pairs with U.
ced_evidence: 1.6.A.3 "adenine nucleotides pair with thymine nucleotides via hydrogen bonds (A-T), and cytosine nucleotides pair with guanine nucleotides via hydrogen bonds (C-G)"

title: Antiparallel DNA double helix
body: DNA drawn as two nucleotide strands running in opposite 5' to 3' orientation, paired by hydrogen bonds between bases.

items.label: Two strands of nucleotides
items.meaning: Form the double helix

items.label: Opposite 5' to 3' orientation
items.meaning: The strands are antiparallel

items.label: A–T pairs
items.meaning: Joined by hydrogen bonds

items.label: C–G pairs
items.meaning: Joined by hydrogen bonds

ced_evidence: 1.6.A.3 "DNA is structured as an antiparallel double helix"

title: Structural differences between DNA and RNA
body: Three structural differences between DNA and RNA.

items.label: Sugar
items.meaning: DNA has deoxyribose; RNA has ribose

items.label: Nitrogenous base
items.meaning: DNA has thymine; RNA has uracil

items.label: Strandedness
items.meaning: DNA is typically double stranded; RNA is typically single stranded

ced_evidence: 1.6.A.4 "Structural differences between DNA and RNA include"

title: Peptide bond
body: A peptide bond is a covalent bond between the carboxyl group (−COOH) of one amino acid and the amine group (−NH2) of the next amino acid, producing a growing peptide chain.
ced_evidence: 1.7.A.1 "covalent (peptide) bonds that form between a carboxyl group (−COOH) of one amino acid and an amine group (−NH2)"

title: Parts of an amino acid
body: An amino acid has a central carbon atom with four groups covalently bound to it.

items.label: Hydrogen atom
items.meaning: Bound to the central carbon

items.label: Carboxyl group
items.meaning: Bound to the central carbon

items.label: Amine group
items.meaning: Bound to the central carbon

items.label: Variable R group
items.meaning: Bound to the central carbon; determines the amino acid's chemical properties

ced_evidence: 1.7.A.2 "a central carbon atom with a hydrogen atom, a carboxyl group, an amine group, and a variable R group"

title: Chemical categories of R groups
body: The R group of an amino acid is categorized by one of three chemical properties; R-group interactions determine the structure and function of that region of the protein.

items.label: Hydrophobic/nonpolar
items.meaning: R-group category

items.label: Hydrophilic/polar
items.meaning: R-group category

items.label: Ionic
items.meaning: R-group category

ced_evidence: 1.7.A.2 "hydrophobic/nonpolar, hydrophilic/polar, or ionic"

title: Four levels of protein structure
body: Protein structure levels in order, all of which determine protein function.

items.label: Primary
items.meaning: Specific sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide; determines overall shape of the protein

items.label: Secondary
items.meaning: Local folding from interactions between atoms of the polypeptide backbone; hydrogen bonding forms alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets

items.label: Tertiary
items.meaning: Three-dimensional shape from hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, ionic interactions, or disulfide bridges

items.label: Quaternary
items.meaning: Arises from interactions between multiple polypeptides

caution: Secondary structure comes from backbone interactions; tertiary structure involves the interactions listed above, including those between R groups. Name the specific interaction type in answers.
ced_evidence: 1.7.A.3–1.7.A.6 "All four levels of a protein structure determine the function of a protein"
